(1) extrinsic goal framing undermines exercise performance because it detracts attention from the task at hand and promotes ego involvement, (2) ego involvement is antithetical with the development of a strong task involvement, and (3) the effect of extrinsic versus intrinsic goal framing on performance can be explained by the mediating effect of task versus ego involvement.

(1) extrinsic goal framing undermines task involvement but enhances ego involvement, and (2) ego involvement, but not task involvement, mediates the effect of extrinsic goal framing, but not intrinsic goal framing, on performance.

understanding the processes that mediate the effect of goal framing on performance and with understanding the role of goal involvement in the development of a positive or a negative task involvement.

ego involvement in an exercise activity is antihetical to optimal performance, whereas an ego approach orientation may be adaptive or maladaptive for performance, depending on the nature of the exercise activity and the type of performance goal that is pursued.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

intrinsic goal framing facilitates exercise performance when it leads individuals to develop a task involvement, whereas extrinsic goal framing undermines exercise performance when it detracts from a task involvement and activates ego involvement.
the negative effects of extrinsic goal framing can only be overcome if the activity is performed in a task involved manner.

intrinsic goal framing is beneficial for performance because it promotes a task involvement and that extrinsic goal framing is detrimental for performance because it detracts from a task involvement and simultaneously promotes an ego involvement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of extrinsic goal framing depend on the extent to which individuals are task or ego involved when engaging in an exercise activity.
it is not the goal orientation or approach orientation per se that determines performance but the goal involvement that is activated by a given goal orientation or approach.
the effects of extrinsic goal framing are not necessarily detrimental to performance, but rather depend on the type of involvement individuals have with the exercise activity.
